paper_metadata.title: Recurrence after a First Unprovoked Cryptogenic/Idiopathic Seizure in Children: A Prospective Study from S˜ao Paulo, Brazil

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the source population, recruitment setting (tertiary hospitals), and explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria. The sample size (n=213) is substantial for this clinical question, and baseline characteristics are well-defined.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: This prospective study was conducted at the Pediatric Epilepsy Clinics of two tertiary hospitals, between September 1989 and August 1998.
items.reasoning: The authors specify the clinical setting and the timeframe for the population of interest.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Most patients were referred from emergency units of both hospitals to our Pediatric Epilepsy Clinics after the first seizure. Some patients were referred from other hospitals.
items.reasoning: The referral pathway is clearly explained, acknowledging the transition from emergency care to specialized clinics.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between September 1989 and August 1998.
items.reasoning: The specific dates for the recruitment window are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Pediatric Epilepsy Clinics of two tertiary hospitals... S˜ao Paulo, Brazil
items.reasoning: The geographic location and the specific type of medical facility are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Children were enrolled in the study if they had the following inclusion criteria: (a) a first unprovoked seizure... (b) maximal interval to the enrollment after the initial episode ≤90 days; and (c) chronologic age between 1 month and 17 years.
items.reasoning: The study uses rigorous, standard definitions for unprovoked seizures and sets a clear 'zero time' window of 90 days.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide a flow diagram or the total number of eligible patients who declined participation, making it impossible to calculate a participation rate.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The study group consisted of 213 patients, 124 boys and 89 girls. Age ranged from 1 month to 17 years (median, 9.4 years).
items.reasoning: Key demographics and clinical variables (age, gender, seizure type) are reported for the baseline cohort.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the follow-up duration is generally adequate, the study lacks a detailed account of patients lost to follow-up. The authors admit that the 90-day enrollment window might have led to missing early recurrences, which is a form of left-censoring bias.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 84% of the patients were followed up for >6 months and 70% of the children for >1 year.
items.reasoning: While a majority were followed, 30% were lost by the 1-year mark, which is a significant proportion in prognosis studies.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (EEG) was measured using standardized protocols (10-20 system, sleep/wake cycles) and interpreted by specialists. CT imaging was also used, though not in all patients.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: The EEG findings were classified as: normal, abnormal with nonepileptiform abnormalities, or abnormal with epileptiform abnormalities.
items.reasoning: The classification of the main prognostic factor is clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: All EEGs were performed on a 16-channel machine by using the 10-20 electrode system... Recording time was ≥20 min.
items.reasoning: Standardized clinical neurophysiology protocols were followed.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were divided in three subgroups according to the chronologic age: younger than 3 years; 3–10 years; and older than 10 years.
items.reasoning: Age categories used are standard in pediatric research.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All EEGs were performed on a 16-channel machine by using the 10-20 electrode system.
items.reasoning: The protocol was consistent across the study population.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Patients had at least one EEG during the first year of the follow-up.
items.reasoning: EEG data appears to be available for the full cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; however, missingness for the primary PF (EEG) was low.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (seizure recurrence) is a clear clinical event. The definition used (24-hour separation) is standard in epilepsy research. While it relies on parental reporting, this is the standard of care for pediatric seizure follow-up.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Recurrence was defined as a new unprovoked seizure occurring ≥24 h after the initial seizure.
items.reasoning: The outcome is explicitly defined using a temporal threshold.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Appointments were scheduled every 6 months, unless a seizure occured.
items.reasoning: Outcome measurement relies on clinical history/parental report, which is standard but carries some risk of recall bias compared to objective monitoring.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Appointments were scheduled every 6 months, unless a seizure occured.
items.reasoning: The follow-up schedule was standardized for the cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling to adjust for potential confounders like age, seizure type, and sleep state. This is the appropriate method to isolate the effect of the primary prognostic factor (EEG).

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: The following variables were analyzed: age, gender, seizure type, number of seizures in the 24 h... sleep state, Todd's paresis, febrile seizure... family history, CT, and EEG.
items.reasoning: The authors measured the standard clinical variables known to influence seizure recurrence.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Seizure type was classified according to the International League Against Epilepsy criteria (14,15).
items.reasoning: Standard international classifications were used for confounding variables.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: At the time of the initial visit, patients underwent a careful history and physical and neurologic examinations
items.reasoning: Confounders were assessed through direct clinical examination and history.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: At the initial visit, patients underwent a careful history and physical and neurologic examinations
items.reasoning: All participants underwent the same baseline assessment protocol.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods were described for missing confounder data.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Treatment was not given to any of the children.
items.reasoning: The study controlled for the confounding effect of medication by excluding treated children, which is a strong design choice for natural history studies.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Univariate and multivariate analyses of the risk factors for recurrence were performed using the Cox proportional hazards model.
items.reasoning: Multivariable adjustment was performed to account for the interplay between variables.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression) are the gold standard for time-to-event prognostic data. The results are reported transparently with confidence intervals and p-values.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Results are displayed as Kaplan– Meier survival curves with the cumulative probability of seizure recurrence plotted as a function of time
items.reasoning: The analytical approach is standard and well-described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Potential predictors of recurrence were compared by using the Cox proportional hazards model in univariate and multivariate analyses.
items.reasoning: The authors tested known clinical predictors in a logical multivariable framework.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Recurrence rates were determined by survival analysis, taking an event as the occurrence of a second seizure.
items.reasoning: Survival analysis is the correct choice for recurrence data where follow-up times vary.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 shows the summary of the results obtained with univariate and multivariate analyses
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings for all variables listed in the methods.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
